To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of the sentinel-node technique for axillary staging of clinically node-negative patients with breast cancer is feasible, safe, and effective.
sentinel node biopsy is an effective procedure that can be used to avoid axillary node dissection in breast-cancer patients.

1) Sentinel node biopsy in breast cancer is an accurate technique to avoid axillary node dissection; 2) Sentinel node biopsy is a reliable procedure in breast cancer with a false negative rate below 10%; 3) Sentinel node biopsy has a low morbidity; 4) Sentinel node biopsy can be performed with a low cost; and 5) Sentinel node biopsy does not affect survival.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sentinel-node biopsy is a useful alternative to axillary dissection, but that axillary dissection is still required for the treatment of clinically node-negative patients who have positive sentinel nodes.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found no difference in overall survival, disease-free survival and distant disease-free survival between sentinel lymph-node biopsy and axillary lymph-node dissection in breast cancers with clinically negative lymphnodes.

we have shown that sentinel-node (SN) biopsy, with or without radioactivity, can be used to avoid axillary lymph-node dissection (ALND) in patients with early breast cancer and clinically negative axillary lymph-nodes, with an accuracy of at least 90%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a sentinel lymph node biopsy in breast cancer patients with clinically negative axillary nodes is safe and effective.

the use of a sentinel-node biopsy to avoid a complete axillary dissection for patients with early breast cancer and clinically negative lymph-nodal basins can be justified on the basis of the reduced morbidity and the improved quality of life that it offers, and it is not necessary to await results from a large, prospective randomised trial to justify the procedure.
